name: Periodontal treatment
lead: Periodontal treatment is the set of professional and home-care measures used to manage periodontal (gum) disease, which ranges from gingivitis to periodontitis with bone loss and tooth loss. Options include home plaque control, professional root-surface instrumentation, surgery for advanced cases, local or systemic antibiotics, lifestyle changes and ongoing maintenance.[1]

For appearance, the payoff is mostly about keeping what a smile is built on: firm, pink, snug-fitting gums and teeth that stay in place. Untreated periodontitis can lead to gum recession that makes teeth look longer, widened gaps between teeth, loose or drifting teeth and eventually tooth loss, so treatment that stabilises the gums helps preserve the visible frame of the smile.[1][14] Treated gums that are free of inflammation also tend to look less red and swollen and bleed less, which is a visible change as well as a health one.[15]

Periodontitis is reported to be the main cause of adult tooth loss worldwide and has been studied for associations with diabetes and cardiovascular disease.[1][3] Randomised trials and meta-analyses have examined whether treating it changes systemic markers, with varying results across outcomes.[2][8][16]

paras: Gum disease starts as gingivitis, an inflammation confined to the gums that is typically reversible with improved plaque control. When the inflammation extends to the ligament and bone that anchor the teeth, it is called periodontitis, which produces deepened gaps (pockets) around the teeth and progressive loss of attachment.[1] Treatment is therefore organised around two goals: removing the bacterial deposits that sustain inflammation, and then keeping them from returning through home care and scheduled maintenance.[1][5]

Which procedures are used depends on how advanced the disease is. A 2017 review framed the topic as a question of how many options exist for one disease, comparing non-surgical and surgical routes and the conditions under which each is used.[5]

Encyclopedic sources list brushing at least twice and flossing daily, regular professional cleaning and non-surgical instrumentation below the gumline, surgery where non-surgical therapy is insufficient, local drug delivery such as tetracycline, and systemic antibiotics in some cases, for which evidence of added benefit is low-certainty. Smoking cessation and diet are also discussed.[1]

Scaling and root planing, often called deep cleaning, removes plaque and calculus from the tooth surface and below the gumline and then smooths the root surfaces so bacteria have less to cling to. It is usually done under local anaesthetic, often one quadrant or half the mouth per visit, with ultrasonic or hand instruments or both.[14] Recognised after-effects include tenderness and tooth sensitivity, and ultrasonic scalers can spread aerosols.[14] A randomised study of cementum preservation compared power-driven and hand instruments, and a trial measured atmospheric contamination during ultrasonic scaling.[17][18]

Where deep pockets remain, periodontal flap surgery may be used to reach the root surface; descriptions of scaling and root planing note that its effect declines in pockets deeper than about 6 mm.[14] Separate procedures address recession that has already occurred. Gingival grafting can move nearby tissue over an exposed root or place tissue taken from the palate, or a donor-derived matrix, over it; the aim is to cover roots and restore a more even gumline.[15] Healing is described as taking a few weeks.[15]

Local antimicrobials and lasers are sometimes added to instrumentation. A narrative review of laser use reported additional clinical benefit when a diode laser accompanied scaling and root planing in moderate to severe periodontitis, and found that an Er:YAG laser produced similar clinical effects to conventional non-surgical therapy.[19] A 2024 randomised trial compared ozonised gels with chlorhexidine in non-surgical treatment.[20]

Adults who have had periodontitis sometimes seek tooth straightening. A randomised controlled trial of 36 periodontally compromised adults (mean age about 30) compared periodontal stabilisation followed by fixed orthodontic treatment with periodontal care alone, evaluating periodontal parameters.[21] A separate randomised trial examined early orthodontic treatment after periodontal surgery.[22]

An 11-year maintenance study examined how residual pockets influence progression of periodontitis and tooth loss.[4] An earlier five-year study of 100 patients with furcation involvement reported that further destruction in those areas could be arrested after treatment.[7]

Randomised trials have tested periodontal treatment against vascular, diabetic and pregnancy outcomes.[2][6][9] The 2007 trial randomised 120 patients with severe periodontitis to intensive treatment or community-based care and measured flow-mediated dilatation of the brachial artery along with inflammatory and coagulation markers.[2] A 12-month randomised trial studied systemic effects in type 2 diabetes,[6] and a meta-analysis of randomised trials examined scaling and root planing against HbA1c and C-reactive protein in people with type 2 diabetes; its authors began by noting the evidence had been inconclusive.[16]

On the mouth itself, a systematic review and meta-analysis of 27 studies with at least 12 months of follow-up found that the share of pockets 3 mm or shallower rose from about 39 percent to 64 percent after non-surgical therapy, while the share of pockets of 5 mm or more fell from about 28 percent to 12 percent; the authors concluded that most pockets are resolved but residual pockets can remain.[23] An 11-year maintenance study examined how those residual pockets influence progression and tooth loss.[4]

Other outcomes have been studied as well. A Mendelian randomisation analysis combined with a randomised trial of non-surgical therapy examined the relationship between periodontitis and hypertension, while a Cochrane review cited in encyclopedic sources found insufficient evidence that treatment lowers blood pressure.[1][24] A 2024 meta-analysis of five randomised trials including 1,984 pregnant women compared treated and untreated groups for preterm birth.[25] A 2023 meta-analysis of 75 articles looked at periodontitis in relation to respiratory diseases and at the effect of periodontal therapy on them.[26] Registered trials include studies of pocket depth change, treatment in diabetes, myocardial infarction and cerebrovascular function.[10][11][12][13]

Instrumentation commonly causes short-term soreness and tooth sensitivity, and removal of root surface can contribute to sensitivity afterwards.[14] Surgical procedures carry the usual risks of oral surgery, such as swelling and discomfort during healing.[15] Alternatives such as chlorhexidine rinses are described as intended for short-term use.[14]

Periodontitis is associated with raised inflammatory markers and with diabetes, with a two-way relationship described between the two; many other associations are not proven causal.[1][3] A randomised trial of 120 patients with severe periodontitis compared intensive treatment with community-based care and measured endothelial function and inflammatory markers.[2] A 12-month randomised trial studied systemic effects of periodontitis treatment in type 2 diabetes,[6] and another trial examined periodontal treatment and preterm birth.[9]

Periodontal care sits between dentistry and cosmetic work. Recession and tooth loss are among the visible consequences of periodontitis, and dental sources describe gum recession as very common, with an estimated 85 percent of people having it on at least one tooth, most often in adults over 40.[15] Because bone loss from periodontitis is described as irreversible while soft tissue can heal, maintenance visits roughly every three to four months are a standard part of care.[1][14]

timeline.event: A five-year evaluation of multirooted tooth treatment is published.[7]
A Leuven group proposes treating the whole mouth in about 24 hours (full-mouth ultrasonic debridement) as an alternative to quadrant-by-quadrant visits.[14]
A randomised trial of periodontal treatment and preterm birth is published.[9]
A trial of intensive periodontal treatment and endothelial function is published.[2]
A 12-month trial in type 2 diabetes is published.[6]

card.summary: The umbrella of professional and home care for gum disease, from deep cleaning to surgery and lifelong maintenance.
card.note: Systemic-health benefits of treatment are studied but mixed or unproven.

quick.overview:
Periodontal treatment covers everything dentists and periodontists do to control gum disease: cleaning below the gumline, surgery in advanced cases, adjunct antibiotics and regular maintenance visits.

It is relevant to appearance because periodontitis can cause receding gums, loose teeth and tooth loss.
quick.mechanism: Treatment aims to remove bacterial plaque and calculus, reduce pocket depth and inflammation, and keep plaque under control through home care and maintenance.
quick.risks: Surgery and instrumentation carry the usual procedural risks such as soreness and sensitivity. Evidence that treating gum disease improves other conditions such as blood pressure is described as insufficient in one Cochrane review.

chain: Plaque and calculus below the gumline are removed
Gum inflammation and pocket depth fall
Gums and supporting bone are kept stable, so teeth stay in place and gums keep their shape
angle.text: Treatment removes the bacterial deposits that drive gum inflammation, so gums look less red and swollen and the tissue holding teeth is preserved. Where recession has already occurred, periodontists also offer grafting procedures that move or add gum tissue over exposed roots.
